transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, what brings me in is... I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t. Important stuff, you know? Like my heart follow-up appointments, and then I forget to call the clinic back to reschedule. 

Though, to be fair, calling that clinic is a full-time job. They have that new automated system where you press one for this, two for that, and you just sit on hold listening to that awful saxophone music. My buddy Lou used to work for the phone company back in the seventies, and he says those systems are actually designed to make you hang up. Makes sense to me. 

But anyway, it's not just the doctors. I'll go to do a repair job—I do a little handyman work here and there since I stopped working—and I'll show up without the right tools. I'll get all the way over there and realize the specific wrench I need is sitting right on my kitchen counter next to the toaster. We just got a new toaster, actually. One of those shiny silver ones with four slots. Burns the bagels every time if you aren't watching it like a hawk. 

But yeah... what were we talking about? Oh, right, just forgetting stuff like that all the time. It's getting really frustrating.
Has this forgetfulness been a problem your entire life, or is this a recent change that has developed over the last few years?

Well, it's definitely not new. It feels like it's been my whole life, really. Even as a boy in grade school, I was always that kid who just couldn’t stay in his seat. I'd blurt out answers all the time and I was constantly getting notes sent home to my parents for talking too much. 

My mother used to keep all those notes in this old wooden cigar box on top of the refrigerator. It was an El Producto box—George Burns used to smoke those, you know. Man, I used to love watching George and Gracie on the television. We had this big, heavy Zenith set in the living room that took about five minutes just to warm up the tubes before you even got a picture. You had to smack the side of it sometimes to stop the screen from rolling. My dad finally fixed it with a piece of folded-up cardboard shoved under the dial. He was a real tinkerer, my dad. Could fix an engine with his eyes closed, but he wouldn't pay a dime for a repairman if he could rig it up himself. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, it's not a recent change at all. I've pretty much always been like this.
Are these difficulties with focus and organization causing problems in more than one area of your life, such as at home, in your relationships, or in your social life?

Yeah, it really is causing trouble all over. Like I was saying before about the doctors... my doctor’s office has had to actually chase me down about those missed heart follow-ups. The nurse who usually calls me, Brenda, she's a real sweetheart. She makes this incredible pecan pie for the charity bake sale every November. You know, the secret to a really good pecan pie is using dark corn syrup, none of that light stuff. My wife used to use the light syrup and it just never set right, always came out runny and soaked right through the crust. But Brenda, she knows exactly what she's doing. 

Anyway, Brenda's always having to call me because I just don't show up. And then, well, down at the senior center... I help out with this repair group there. We fix up chairs and little things for folks. But it’s gotten to where they just can’t count on me the way they used to. I'll completely forget it's my day to be there, or I'll show up and start taking apart the breakroom coffee machine instead of doing what I'm supposed to. That coffee machine is a total piece of junk, by the way. It's one of those old percolators that makes the coffee taste like burnt pennies. You ever had coffee like that? It just coats your tongue and ruins your whole morning. But yeah, I guess it's definitely messing things up for me with the group and the doctors.
Do you still find it difficult to sit still for long periods, or do you feel a need to be constantly moving?

Oh, absolutely. I just can't sit still. Especially lately. Since I've had to slow down on my walks and my little repair projects, sitting around just makes me feel like I've got a motor running inside me and nowhere good to put all that energy. 

It reminds me of this old Ford pickup I used to have in my twenties. Beautiful truck, cherry red, but the idle was always set too high. You'd be sitting at a red light and the whole cab would just vibrate, like it was begging to take off. I tried adjusting the carburetor myself a dozen times, but I could never get it quite right. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he told me it was the timing belt, but what did he know? He drove a station wagon with wood paneling on the side. You don't see those anymore, do you? The wood paneling, I mean. It always peeled off after a few years anyway, looked terrible. 

But yeah... sitting still is just awful for me. I always feel like I need to be doing something with my hands or getting up to check on something.
When you are working on those repair projects, do you find that you often overlook small details or make careless mistakes in your work?

Well, no, not really. I don't think I make careless mistakes when I'm fixing things. I mean, I might get distracted and start working on something else entirely, but the work I actually do is pretty solid. 

Take that coffee machine down at the center, for example. I didn't get it put all the way back together last time because I realized the heating element was completely shot. It's one of those old aluminum coils, you know? They don't make them like that anymore. Now everything is just cheap plastic and circuit boards that fry if you look at them wrong. My grandson bought this fancy espresso maker—cost him an arm and a leg, probably more than my first car did. And what happens? Three months in, a little green light starts blinking and the whole thing just shuts down. Can't even make a regular cup of joe. He had to box the whole thing up and mail it to some warehouse in New Jersey just to get it looked at. In the old days, you could just pop the back off, find the loose wire, and solder it yourself. I've got a soldering iron in my garage that I've had since 1975. Still works perfectly. 

But no, I wouldn't say I make careless mistakes. I just... well, I might not always finish what I started because I find something else that needs fixing first.
When you are in social situations or talking with others, do you often find that you interrupt people, finish their sentences, or have a hard time waiting for your turn to speak?

Well, yeah, I suppose I do that a fair bit. Like down at the senior center, if I hear folks at the next table discussing a repair project or arguing over a hand of pinochle, I'll just jump right in and give them my two cents before anyone even asks me. I can usually tell right after I do it that I just barged in where I wasn't invited, but it just slips out. 

Speaking of pinochle, they use these awful plastic-coated cards down there now. They stick together when the humidity gets high. My uncle Arthur, he taught me how to play cards, and he swore by those old paper Bicycle decks. He used to say you could tell a lot about a man by how he shuffled a deck of cards. Uncle Arthur was a character, let me tell you. He worked on the railroad for forty years, lost half his left index finger coupling cars in the rail yard in Chicago. Never slowed him down, though. He could still deal a hand of poker faster than anyone I ever met. He had this little trick where he'd flip the cards... 

But yeah, what were we talking about? Oh, right, interrupting. Yeah, I definitely have a bad habit of jumping into other people's business before they ask for my opinion.
Looking back at your life, have you consistently struggled with both the focus issues and the need to be constantly moving, or has one of those been a much bigger problem for you than the other?

Well, it's really always been the moving around and the talking that got me in the most trouble. Even as a boy in grade school, I was the kid who just couldn’t stay in his seat. I always blurted out answers before the teacher even called on anyone, and I got so many notes sent home for talking too much. 

I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she actually started pinning those notes right to my jacket collar with a safety pin so I couldn't "accidentally" lose them on the walk home. We had to walk a good two miles back then, right down Elm Street. Elm Street used to have these massive, beautiful elm trees, right up until the Dutch elm disease wiped them all out in the sixties. It was a real shame, you know? The whole neighborhood looked completely different after the city came and chopped them down. Just bare. 

My dad actually saved some of the wood from the one they took down in our front yard. He tried to build a coffee table out of it in the garage. But elm is a really tough wood to work with. The grain is all interlocked, so it splits if you don't know exactly what you're doing with the saw. He spent three weekends swearing at that wood before he ended up just tossing the whole thing in the wood chipper. We had this big old gas-powered chipper back then, loud as a jet engine. You'd have to wear earplugs just to stand in the driveway... 

But, uh, anyway. What was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, the moving around and the blurting things out. That's always been the biggest issue for me, hands down, my whole life.
